claim: Doxorubicin (Doxo) causes buildup of senescent cells in skeletal muscle, leading to the inhibition of tissue regeneration.
source: In the context of skeletal muscle, it is known that agents used for chemotherapy such as Doxorubicin (Doxo) cause buildup of senescent cells, leading to the inhibition of tissue regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to existing literature as indicated by the context of 'it is known'.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 is an electrophilic lipid produced by the non-enzymatic dehydration of the prostaglandin PGD2.
source: Arachidonic acid-derived lipids have been shown to accumulate within senescent cells, specifically 15d-PGJ2, which is an electrophilic lipid produced by the non-enzymatic dehydration of the prostaglandin PGD2.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established biochemical knowledge about prostaglandin metabolism.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 is released by Doxo-induced senescent cells as an SASP factor.
source: This study shows that 15d-PGJ2 is also released by Doxo-induced senescent cells as an SASP factor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J demonstrating increased 15d-PGJ2 release from senescent cells.

claim: Treatment of skeletal muscle myoblasts with the conditioned medium from senescent cells inhibits myoblast fusion during differentiation.
source: Treatment of skeletal muscle myoblasts with the conditioned medium from these senescent cells inhibits myoblast fusion during differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A measuring fusion index.

claim: Inhibition of L-PTGDS diminishes the release of 15d-PGJ2 by senescent cells and restores muscle differentiation.
source: Inhibition of L-PTGDS, the enzyme that synthesizes PGD2, diminishes the release of 15d-PGJ2 by senescent cells and restores muscle differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A using AT-56 inhibitor treatment.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 post-translationally modifies Cys184 of HRas in C2C12 mouse skeletal myoblasts.
source: We further show that this lipid post-translationally modifies Cys184 of HRas in C2C12 mouse skeletal myoblasts
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A using biotinylated 15d-PGJ2 and streptavidin pulldown.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 modification of HRas causes a reduction in the localization of HRas to the Golgi.
source: We further show that this lipid post-translationally modifies Cys184 of HRas in C2C12 mouse skeletal myoblasts, causing a reduction in the localization of HRas to the Golgi
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B measuring HRas distribution between Golgi and plasma membrane.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 modification of HRas increases HRas binding to Ras Binding Domain (RBD) of RAF Kinase (RAF-RBD).
source: We further show that this lipid post-translationally modifies Cys184 of HRas in C2C12 mouse skeletal myoblasts, causing a reduction in the localization of HRas to the Golgi, increased HRas binding to Ras Binding Domain (RBD) of RAF Kinase (RAF-RBD)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-D using FRET measurements.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 modification of HRas activates cellular Mitogen Activated Protein (MAP) kinase–Extracellular Signal Regulated Kinase (Erk) signaling but not the Akt signaling.
source: We further show that this lipid post-translationally modifies Cys184 of HRas in C2C12 mouse skeletal myoblasts, causing a reduction in the localization of HRas to the Golgi, increased HRas binding to Ras Binding Domain (RBD) of RAF Kinase (RAF-RBD), and activation of cellular Mitogen Activated Protein (MAP) kinase–Extracellular Signal Regulated Kinase (Erk) signaling (but not the Akt signaling).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E-F for Erk phosphorylation and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C for Akt phosphorylation.

claim: Mutating C184 of HRas prevents the ability of 15d-PGJ2 to inhibit the differentiation of muscle cells.
source: Mutating C184 of HRas prevents the ability of 15d-PGJ2 to inhibit the differentiation of muscle cells and control the activity of HRas.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D-E measuring differentiation markers in HRas C184S mutant cells.

claim: Doxo treatment increases expression of p21 in mouse Gastrocnemius muscles.
source: We observed an increase in the expression of p21 and increased nuclear levels of the DNA damage marker γH2A.X in mouse Gastrocnemius muscles (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Doxo treatment increases nuclear levels of the DNA damage marker γH2A.X in mouse Gastrocnemius muscles.
source: We observed an increase in the expression of p21 and increased nuclear levels of the DNA damage marker γH2A.X in mouse Gastrocnemius muscles (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Doxo treatment significantly increases mRNA levels of senescence markers (Cdkn1a and Cdkn2a) in skeletal muscles of mice.
source: We also observed a significant increase in the mRNA levels of known senescence markers (Cdkn1a and Cdkn2a), SASP factors (Cxcl1, Cxcl2, Tnfa, Il6, and Tgfb1) in skeletal muscles of mice treated with Doxo compared to that of mice treated with saline (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Doxo treatment significantly increases mRNA levels of SASP factors (Cxcl1, Cxcl2, Tnfa, Il6, and Tgfb1) in skeletal muscles of mice.
source: We also observed a significant increase in the mRNA levels of known senescence markers (Cdkn1a and Cdkn2a), SASP factors (Cxcl1, Cxcl2, Tnfa, Il6, and Tgfb1) in skeletal muscles of mice treated with Doxo compared to that of mice treated with saline (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Doxo treatment induces senescence in hindlimb skeletal muscles of B6J mice.
source: Therefore, we injected B6J mice intraperitoneally with Doxo (5 mg/kg) every 3 days for 9 days and observed induction of DNA damage-mediated senescence in hindlimb skeletal muscles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple senescence markers shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: Doxo treatment increases nuclear area in C2C12 myoblasts.
source: We treated C2C12 myoblasts with Doxo (150 nM) and observed a significant increase in the size of the nuclei (Figure 1D)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Doxo treatment causes flattened cell morphology with an increase in cell size in C2C12 myoblasts.
source: We treated C2C12 myoblasts with Doxo (150 nM) and observed a significant increase in the size of the nuclei (Figure 1D), flattened cell morphology with an increase in the cell size (Figure 1E)
evidence: This claim is supported by widefield microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Doxo treatment significantly increases mRNA levels of cell cycle inhibitor Cdkn1a and SASP factors Il6 and Tgfb in C2C12 cells.
source: We treated C2C12 myoblasts with Doxo (150 nM) and observed a significant increase in the size of the nuclei (Figure 1D), flattened cell morphology with an increase in the cell size (Figure 1E), a significant increase in the mRNA levels of cell cycle inhibitor Cdkn1a and SASP factors Il6 and Tgfb (Figure 1F)
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Doxo treatment significantly increases protein levels of p21 in C2C12 cells.
source: We treated C2C12 myoblasts with Doxo (150 nM) and observed a significant increase in the size of the nuclei (Figure 1D), flattened cell morphology with an increase in the cell size (Figure 1E), a significant increase in the mRNA levels of cell cycle inhibitor Cdkn1a and SASP factors Il6 and Tgfb (Figure 1F), a significant increase in the protein levels of p21 (Figure 1G)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Doxo treatment increases levels of SA β-gal in C2C12 cells.
source: We treated C2C12 myoblasts with Doxo (150 nM) and observed a significant increase in the size of the nuclei (Figure 1D), flattened cell morphology with an increase in the cell size (Figure 1E), a significant increase in the mRNA levels of cell cycle inhibitor Cdkn1a and SASP factors Il6 and Tgfb (Figure 1F), a significant increase in the protein levels of p21 (Figure 1G), and an increase in the levels of SA β-gal (Figure 1H) in C2C12 cells treated with Doxo.
evidence: This claim is supported by X-gal staining data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: C2C12 cells undergo senescence upon treatment with Doxo.
source: These observations suggest that C2C12 cells undergo senescence upon treatment with Doxo.
evidence: This claim is inferred from multiple senescence markers shown in Figure 1D-H.

claim: Doxo treatment significantly increases mRNA levels of Ptgs1, Ptgs2, and Ptgds enzymes in skeletal muscle of mice.
source: We observed a significant increase in the mRNA levels of Ptgs1, Ptgs2, and Ptgds enzymes in the skeletal muscle of mice treated with Doxo (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Doxo treatment causes time-dependent increase in mRNA levels of Ptgs1, Ptgs2, Ptgds, and Ptges enzymes in C2C12 cells.
source: We also observed a time-dependent increase in the mRNA levels of Ptgs1, Ptgs2, Ptgds, and Ptges enzymes in C2C12 cells treated with Doxo compared to Day 0 (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Expression of enzyme Ptges was elevated on Day 4 in Doxo-treated C2C12 cells.
source: Expression of enzyme Ptges was elevated on Day 4, whereas the expression of prostaglandin D synthase (Ptgds) increased only after Day 8, reaching maximum expression on Day 12.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Expression of prostaglandin D synthase (Ptgds) increased only after Day 8, reaching maximum expression on Day 12 in Doxo-treated C2C12 cells.
source: Expression of enzyme Ptges was elevated on Day 4, whereas the expression of prostaglandin D synthase (Ptgds) increased only after Day 8, reaching maximum expression on Day 12.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: There is a significant increase (~40-fold) in the concentration of 15d-PGJ2 in the conditioned medium from senescent cells compared to quiescent cells.
source: We observed a significant increase (~40-fold) in the concentration of 15d-PGJ2 in the conditioned medium from senescent cells as compared to that in quiescent cells (Figure 1J, Figure 1—source data 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Senescent C2C12 cells release 15d-PGJ2 in the medium.
source: This suggests that senescent C2C12 cells release 15d-PGJ2 in the medium.
evidence: This claim is inferred from mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 has been shown to inhibit the differentiation of myoblasts.
source: 15d-PGJ2 (the final non-enzymatic dehydration product of PGD2) has been shown to inhibit the differentiation of myoblasts (Hunter et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hunter et al., 2001.

claim: Conditioned medium of senescent cells inhibits the differentiation of myoblasts in myotonic dystrophy type 1.
source: Conditioned medium of senescent cells inhibits the differentiation of myoblasts in myotonic dystrophy type 1 (Conte et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Conte et al., 2023.

claim: There is a significant decrease (~20%) in the fusion index of C2C12 myoblasts treated with the conditioned medium of senescent cells.
source: We observed a significant decrease (~20%) in the fusion index of the C2C12 myoblasts treated with the conditioned medium of senescent cells (Figure 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: SASP factors decrease the differentiation of myoblasts.
source: We observed a significant decrease (~20%) in the fusion index of the C2C12 myoblasts treated with the conditioned medium of senescent cells (Figure 2A), suggesting that SASP factors decrease the differentiation of myoblasts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the effect of conditioned medium on fusion index shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The decrease in myoblast differentiation by senescent cell conditioned medium is rescued by AT-56 treatment.
source: This decrease in the inhibition was rescued in myoblasts treated with the conditioned medium of senescent cells treated with AT-56 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Prostaglandins PGD2/15d-PGJ2 released by senescent cells as SASP factors can inhibit the differentiation of myoblasts.
source: This suggests that prostaglandins PGD2/15d-PGJ2 released by senescent cells as SASP factors can inhibit the differentiation of myoblasts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the rescue of differentiation by AT-56 treatment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 treatment causes a significant decrease in the proliferation of C2C12 cells.
source: We treated C2C12 myoblasts with 15d-PGJ2 (10 µM) or DMSO in DMEM (Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium)10% serum medium for 72 hr and observed a significant decrease in the proliferation of C2C12 cells after treatment with 15d-PGJ2 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The doubling time of C2C12 cells was increased upon treatment with 15d-PGJ2 (57.24 hr) compared to DMSO (13.76 hr).
source: The doubling time of C2C12 cells was also increased upon treatment with 15d-PGJ2 (57.24 hr) compared to DMSO (13.76 hr).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 decreases the proliferation of C2C12 myoblasts.
source: This suggests that 15d-PGJ2 decreases the proliferation of C2C12 myoblasts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the doubling time and cell count data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 was not cytotoxic up to 5 µM in the C2C12 differentiation medium.
source: We judged that 15d-PGJ2 was not cytotoxic up to 5 µM in the C2C12 differentiation medium (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by MTT viability assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 treatment causes a dose-dependent decrease in the mRNA levels of Myod1, Myog, and Myhc in differentiating C2C12 cells.
source: We observed a dose-dependent decrease in the mRNA levels of Myod1, Myog, and Myhc in differentiating C2C12 cells after treatment with 15d-PGJ2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There is a significant decrease in the number of nuclei in individual MHC+ve fiber (~75%) in C2C12 cells treated with 15d-PGJ2 (4 µM) compared to DMSO.
source: There was a significant decrease in the no. of nuclei in individual MHC+ve fiber (~75%) in C2C12 cells treated with 15d-PGJ2 (4 µM) compared to DMSO (Figure 2D)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 treatment causes a decrease in the fusion of myoblasts in myotubes.
source: There was a significant decrease in the no. of nuclei in individual MHC+ve fiber (~75%) in C2C12 cells treated with 15d-PGJ2 (4 µM) compared to DMSO (Figure 2D), suggesting a decrease in the fusion of myoblasts in myotubes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the decrease in nuclei per fiber shown in Figure 2D.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 treatment causes a dose-dependent decrease in the protein levels of MHC in differentiating primary human myoblasts.
source: We also observed a dose-dependent decrease in the protein levels of MHC in differentiating primary human myoblasts upon treatment with 15d-PGJ2 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 inhibits the differentiation of both mouse and human myoblasts.
source: Together, these observations suggest that 15d-PGJ2 inhibits the differentiation of both mouse and human myoblasts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from data shown in Figures 2C-E.

claim: HRas was identified to be covalently modified by 15d-PGJ2 at cysteine 184 in NIH3T3 and Cos1 cells.
source: HRas was identified to be covalently modified by 15d-PGJ2 at cysteine 184 in NIH3T3 and Cos1 cells (Oliva et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Oliva et al., 2003.

claim: There is a significant increase (~3.5-fold) in the pulldown of HRas upon treatment with 15d-PGJ2-Biotin compared to DMSO.
source: We observed a significant increase (~3.5-fold) in the pulldown of HRas upon treatment with 15d-PGJ2-Biotin compared to DMSO (Figure 3A)
evidence: This claim is supported by streptavidin immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There is an interaction between 15d-PGJ2 and HRas.
source: We observed a significant increase (~3.5-fold) in the pulldown of HRas upon treatment with 15d-PGJ2-Biotin compared to DMSO (Figure 3A), suggesting an interaction between 15d-PGJ2 and HRas.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pulldown data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The intensity of EGFP-tagged HRas was significantly decreased in cells expressing the C184S mutant (~80% decrease compared to HRas WT) but not in those expressing the C181S mutant.
source: We observed that the intensity of EGFP-tagged HRas was significantly decreased in cells expressing the C184S mutant (~80% decrease compared to HRas WT) but not in those expressing the C181S mutant (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by streptavidin immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 covalently modifies HRas at cysteine 184 in C2C12 cells.
source: This suggests that 15d-PGJ2 covalently modifies HRas at cysteine 184 in C2C12 cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential pulldown of HRas mutants shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There is a significant increase (~30%) in the mean acceptor normalized FRET index upon treatment with 15d-PGJ2 in cells expressing HRas WT.
source: We observed a significant increase (~30%) in the mean acceptor normalized FRET index upon treatment with 15d-PGJ2 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 activates HRas.
source: We observed a significant increase (~30%) in the mean acceptor normalized FRET index upon treatment with 15d-PGJ2 (Figure 3C). This suggests that 15d-PGJ2 activates HRas.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the FRET data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There is a significant increase (~40%) in the mean acceptor normalized FRET index in cells expressing EGFP-HRas C181S upon treatment with 15d-PGJ2 but not in cells expressing EGFP-HRas C184S.
source: We observed a significant increase (~40%) in the mean acceptor normalized FRET index in cells expressing EGFP-HRas C181S upon treatment with 15d-PGJ2 but not in cells expressing EGFP-HRas C184S (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET microscopy data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Activation of HRas by 15d-PGJ2 occurs in a cysteine 184-dependent manner.
source: These observations suggest that activation of HRas by 15d-PGJ2 occurs in a cysteine 184-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential FRET response in HRas mutants shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 treatment causes a dose-dependent increase in the phosphorylation of Erk (T202/Y204) (42 kDa) but not of Erk (44 kDa).
source: We treated C2C12 cells with 15d-PGJ2 (5 and 10 µM) or DMSO for 1 hr (after 24 hr of serum starvation) and observed a dose-dependent increase in the phosphorylation of Erk (T202/Y204) (42 kDa) but not of Erk (44 kDa) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 treatment does not increase the phosphorylation of Akt (S473) in C2C12 cells.
source: We did not observe an increase in the phosphorylation of Akt (S473) in C2C12 cells after treatment with 15d-PGJ2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 activates the MAPK signaling pathway, but not the PI3K signaling pathway.
source: These observations suggest that 15d-PGJ2 activates the MAPK signaling pathway, but not the PI3K signaling pathway.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential phosphorylation of Erk and Akt shown in Figures 3E and 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The phosphorylation of Erk (42 and 44 kDa) in C2C12 cells treated with 9,10-dihydro-15d-PGJ2 was significantly reduced (~70%) compared to treatment with 15d-PGJ2.
source: We observed that the phosphorylation of Erk (42 and 44 kDa) in C2C12 cells treated with 9,10-dihydro-15d-PGJ2 was significantly reduced (~70%) as compared to the treatment with 15d-PGJ2 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 activates the HRas–MAPK signaling pathway via the electrophilic center in its cyclopentenone ring.
source: This shows that 15d-PGJ2 activates the HRas–MAPK signaling pathway via the electrophilic center in its cyclopentenone ring.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the reduced Erk phosphorylation with 9,10-dihydro-15d-PGJ2 shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Reversible palmitoylation of cysteine 181 and 184 in the C-terminal tail of HRas regulates intracellular distribution and signaling of HRas.
source: Reversible palmitoylation of cysteine 181 and 184 in the C-terminal tail of HRas regulates intracellular distribution and signaling of HRas.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established knowledge about HRas palmitoylation.

claim: Inhibition of palmitoylation of the C-terminal cysteine 181 causes accumulation of HRas at the Golgi compared to the plasma membrane and alters activity.
source: Inhibition of palmitoylation of the C-terminal cysteine 181, either by a palmitoylation inhibitor 2-bromopalmitate or by mutation to serine, causes accumulation of HRas at the Golgi compared to the plasma membrane and alters activity (Rocks et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rocks et al., 2005.

claim: There is a significant decrease (~20%) in the Rmean of C2C12 cells expressing the wild-type HRas after treatment with 15d-PGJ2.
source: We measured the intracellular distribution of HRas between the Golgi and the plasma membrane in C2C12 cells after treatment with 15d-PGJ2 (10 µM) for 24 hr in DMEM 10% serum medium and observed a significant decrease (~20%) in the Rmean of C2C12 cells expressing the wild-type HRas after treatment with 15d-PGJ2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There is no change in the Rmean of C2C12 cells expressing HRas C181S or HRas C184S after treatment with 15d-PGJ2.
source: However, we did not observe a change in the Rmean of C2C12 cells expressing HRas C181S or HRas C184S after treatment with 15d-PGJ2 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 increases the localization of HRas at the plasma membrane as compared to that in the Golgi in an HRas C-terminal cysteine-dependent manner.
source: These observations suggest that 15d-PGJ2 increases the localization of HRas at the plasma membrane as compared to that in the Golgi in an HRas C-terminal cysteine-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential Rmean changes in HRas mutants shown in Figures 4B-C.

claim: HRas inhibits the differentiation of C2C12 myoblasts.
source: HRas inhibits the differentiation of C2C12 myoblasts (Engler et al., 2021; Konieczny et al., 1989; Lassar et al., 1989; Lee et al., 2010; Olson et al., 1987; Scholz et al., 2009; van der Burgt et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: There is a decrease in the levels of mRNA of Myhc in C2C12 cells expressing HRas WT and HRas C181S after 5 days of treatment with 15d-PGJ2, but not in cells expressing HRas C184S.
source: We observed a decrease in the levels of mRNA of Myhc in C2C12 cells expressing HRas WT and HRas C181S after 5 days of treatment with 15d-PGJ2. We did not observe this in expressing HRas C184S (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There is a significant decrease in the protein levels of MHC in differentiating C2C12 cells expressing HRas WT and HRas C181S after treatment with 15d-PGJ2.
source: We also observed a significant decrease in the protein levels of MHC in differentiating C2C12 cells expressing HRas WT and HRas C181S after treatment with 15d-PGJ2 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The decrease in MHC protein levels by 15d-PGJ2 was partially rescued in cells expressing HRas C184S.
source: This decrease was partially rescued in cells expressing HRas C184S (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The inhibition of myoblast differentiation by 15d-PGJ2 depends on modification of HRas C-terminal cysteine 184.
source: These observations suggest that the inhibition of myoblast differentiation by 15d-PGJ2 depends on modification of HRas C-terminal cysteine 184.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the rescue of differentiation in HRas C184S mutant shown in Figures 4D-E.

claim: Senescent cells are characterized by increased expression of senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity (SA β-gal) and cell cycle inhibitors such as p21 or p16.
source: Senescent cells are characterized by multiple features such as increased expression of senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity (SA β-gal) and cell cycle inhibitors such as p21 or p16.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about senescence markers.

claim: Senescent cells accumulate with tissue damage and dysregulate tissue homeostasis.
source: They accumulate with tissue damage and dysregulate tissue homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about senescence.

claim: Senescent cells influence the neighboring cells via numerous secreted factors which form the senescence-associated secreted phenotype (SASP).
source: Senescent cells influence the neighboring cells via numerous secreted factors which form the senescence-associated secreted phenotype (SASP).
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about SASP.

claim: Lipids are emerging as a key component of SASP that can control tissue homeostasis.
source: Lipids are emerging as a key component of SASP that can control tissue homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by recent literature on SASP components.

claim: Arachidonic acid-derived lipids have been shown to accumulate within senescent cells.
source: Arachidonic acid-derived lipids have been shown to accumulate within senescent cells, specifically 15d-PGJ2
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to existing literature.

claim: Senescent cells are important drivers of aging and damage-associated loss of tissue homeostasis.
source: Senescent cells are important drivers of aging and damage-associated loss of tissue homeostasis (Childs et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Childs et al., 2015.

claim: Treatment with chemotherapeutics such as Doxorubicin causes widespread cellular senescence which inhibits tissue homeostasis and regeneration, including in skeletal muscles.
source: Anti-cancer chemotherapy presents an important context where treatment with chemotherapeutics such as Doxorubicin (Doxo) causes widespread cellular senescence which inhibits tissue homeostasis and regeneration, including in skeletal muscles (Francis et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Francis et al., 2022.

claim: Doxo causes systemic inflammation and leads to the emergence of senescent cells across tissues.
source: It has been shown that Doxo causes systemic inflammation and leads to the emergence of senescent cells across tissues (Di Leonardo et al., 1994; Hu and Zhang, 2019; Robles and Adami, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Di Leonardo et al., 1994; Hu and Zhang, 2019; Robles and Adami, 1998.

claim: Senescent cells negatively affect tissue homeostasis and regeneration by releasing factors including proteins and small molecules.
source: Senescent cells negatively affect tissue homeostasis and regeneration by releasing factors including proteins like growth factors, matrix metalloproteases, cytokines, and chemokines, and small molecules like fatty acid derivatives (Campisi, 2005; Coppé et al., 2010; Dilley et al., 2003; Krtolica et al., 2001; Parrinello et al., 2005; Shelton et al., 1999; Yang et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: SASP factors and their mechanisms of action vary depending on cellular and tissue contexts.
source: It is expected that these SASP factors and their mechanisms of action will vary depending on cellular and tissue contexts.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the complexity of SASP.

claim: Identifying SASP factors and their underlying mechanistic targets will be critical for building an understanding of how senescent cells control tissue homeostasis.
source: Identifying SASP factors and their underlying mechanistic targets will be critical for building an understanding of how senescent cells control tissue homeostasis (Coppé et al., 2010; Davalos et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Coppé et al., 2010; Davalos et al., 2010.

claim: Lipids are a less explored family of SASP factors.
source: Lipids are a less explored family of SASP factors, and it is important to understand how they affect tissue regeneration (Hamsanathan and Gurkar, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hamsanathan and Gurkar, 2022.

claim: Senescent cells have increased intracellular levels of prostaglandin 15d-PGJ2.
source: We have previously shown that senescent cells have increased intracellular levels of prostaglandin 15d-PGJ2 (Wiley et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wiley et al., 2021.

claim: PGD2 and 15d-PGJ2 have been shown to negatively regulate muscle differentiation via mechanisms that do not depend on a cognate receptor.
source: In the context of skeletal muscle, PGD2 and 15d-PGJ2 have been shown to negatively regulate muscle differentiation via mechanisms that do not depend on a cognate receptor (Hunter et al., 2001; Veliça et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hunter et al., 2001; Veliça et al., 2010.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 has been previously shown to covalently modify multiple proteins like MAPK1, MCM4, EIF4A-I, PKM1, GFAP, etc. in endothelial and neuronal cells.
source: 15d-PGJ2 has been previously shown to covalently modify multiple proteins like MAPK1, MCM4, EIF4A-I, PKM1, GFAP, etc. in endothelial and neuronal cells (Marcone and Fitzgerald, 2013; Yamamoto et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Marcone and Fitzgerald, 2013; Yamamoto et al., 2011.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 was shown to be covalently modifying HRas in NIH3T3, Cos1, and IMR90 cell lines.
source: 15d-PGJ2 was shown to be covalently modifying HRas in NIH3T3, Cos1, and IMR90 cell lines (Oliva et al., 2003; Wiley et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Oliva et al., 2003; Wiley et al., 2021.

claim: HRas belongs to the Ras superfamily of small molecule GTPases and is a known regulator of key cellular processes.
source: We investigated HRas as a possible effector of 15d-PGJ2 because (1) HRas belongs to the Ras superfamily of small molecule GTPases and is a known regulator of key cellular processes (Davis et al., 1983; Harvey, 1964; Kirsten and Mayer, 1967; Vetter and Wittinghofer, 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Constitutively active HRas mutant (HRas V12) has been shown to inhibit the differentiation of myoblasts by inhibiting MyoD and Myogenin expression.

claim: Skeletal and cardiac myopathies are observed in individuals carrying constitutively active mutants of HRas.

claim: Prostaglandins secreted as SASP inhibit the differentiation of myoblasts via a mechanism involving HRas modification.

claim: Treatment with Doxo induces senescence in cancer cells like HeLa cells.

source: A study has shown that prostaglandin PGD2 inhibits differentiation of C2C12 myoblasts (Veliça et al., 2010)

source: This observation suggested that PGD2 might inhibit the differentiation of myoblasts by a receptor-independent mechanism, possibly by its spontaneous non-enzymatic dehydration to 15d-PGJ2.

source: 15d-PGJ2 has been suggested to be an endogenous ligand of Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) (Li et al., 2019).

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Slanovc et al., 2024.

claim: 15d-PGJ2 contains an electrophilic cyclopentenone ring in its structure, allowing 15d-PGJ2 to covalently modify and form Michael adducts with cysteine residues of proteins.

claim: A proteomic study in endothelial cells showed biotinylated 15d-PGJ2 covalently modified over 300 proteins.
source: A previous proteomic study in endothelial cells showed biotinylated 15d-PGJ2 covalently modified over 300 proteins, which regulate several physiological processes including cell cycle (MAPK1, MCM4), cell metabolism (fatty acid synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase), apoptosis (PDCD6I), translation (elongation factor 1 and 2, EIF4A-I), intracellular transport (Importin subunit β1, Exportin 2, Kinesin 1 heavy chain) (Marcone and Fitzgerald, 2013).

claim: A proteomic study in neuronal cells suggested that 15d-PGJ2 modifies several proteins including chaperone HSP8A, glycolytic proteins, and cytoskeleton proteins.

source: Modification by 15d-PGJ2 led to the activation of HRas, judged by an increase in GTP-bound HRas.

source: We showed that covalent modification of HRas by 15d-PGJ2 via the electrophilic cyclopentenone ring activates HRas (Figure 3C, D) and activates the HRas–MAPK pathway, demonstrated by an increase in the phosphorylation of Erk after treatment with 15d-PGJ2 (Figure 3E, F).

claim: MAPK and PI3K pathways are known regulators of muscle differentiation.
source: MAPK and PI3K pathways are known regulators of muscle differentiation (Bennett and Tonks, 1997; Rommel et al., 1999)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bennett and Tonks, 1997; Rommel et al., 1999.

claim: Inhibition of the RAF–MEK–Erk pathway or activation of the PI3K pathway promotes the differentiation of myoblasts.
source: MAPK and PI3K pathways are known regulators of muscle differentiation (Bennett and Tonks, 1997; Rommel et al., 1999), where inhibition of the RAF–Mitogen-Activated Protein Kinase Kinase (MEK)–Erk pathway or activation of the PI3K pathway promotes the differentiation of myoblasts.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bennett and Tonks, 1997; Rommel et al., 1999.

claim: Preferential activation of the HRas–MAPK pathway over the HRas–PI3K pathway after treatment with 15d-PGJ2 can be a possible mechanism by which 15d-PGJ2 can inhibit the differentiation of myoblasts.
source: Preferential activation of the HRas–MAPK pathway over the HRas–PI3K pathway after treatment with 15d-PGJ2 can be a possible mechanism by which 15d-PGJ2 can inhibit the differentiation of myoblasts.

claim: HRas is known to regulate the differentiation of myoblasts in different contexts.
source: HRas is known to regulate the differentiation of myoblasts in different contexts.

claim: The inhibition of differentiation of myoblasts by 15d-PGJ2 is partially dependent on the covalent modification of HRas by 15d-PGJ2.

claim: Intracellular localization of HRas maintains two distinct pools of HRas activity, where the plasma membrane pool shows a faster activation followed by short kinetics and the Golgi pool shows a slower activation but a sustained activation.

evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

source: We showed that the covalent modification of HRas by 15d-PGJ2 alters the intracellular distribution of HRas.

source: We showed that the covalent modification of HRas by 15d-PGJ2 leads to an increase in the localization of the wild-type HRas at the plasma membrane compared to the Golgi (Figure 4B).

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to existing literature.
